claims.source: As previously demonstrated (Wilkens et al., 2001), potentiation of L-type Ca2+ channels by DHP agonist Bay K 8644 and strong depolarizations occurs via distinct mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The shift in mode of gating, also referred to as 'mode 2' gating is characterized at the single-channel level by high open probability (PO) and long mean open times.
claims.source: The shift in mode of gating, also referred to as 'mode 2' gating is characterized at the single-channel level by high open probability (PO) and long mean open times (Pietrobon and Hess, 1990).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Depolarization-induced entry into mode 2 is reflected by increased Ca2+ currents as well as tail currents with slower rate of current decay.
claims.source: Depolarization-induced entry into mode 2 is reflected by increased Ca2+ currents as well as tail currents with slower rate of current decay.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about L-type Ca2+ channel behavior.

claims.claim: Recording conditions known to potentiate L-type inward Ca2+ currents through the wt DHPR were unable to evoke Ca2+ currents through the mutant DHPR(N617D) in the ncDHPR mouse model.
claims.source: Altogether, our results demonstrate that recording conditions known to potentiate L-type inward Ca2+ currents through the wt DHPR were unable to evoke Ca2+ currents through the mutant DHPR(N617D) in the ncDHPR mouse model.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Out of the three mutant mammalian DHPR Ca2+ channels with ablated Ca2+ conducting ability under standard recording conditions (R174W, E1014K, and N617D), only the voltage-sensor mutant R174W opened partially and produced tail currents under (±)Bay K 8644 administration.
claims.source: Out of the three, so far described mutant mammalian DHPR Ca2+ channels with ablated Ca2+ conducting ability under standard recording conditions, namely R174W (Eltit et al., 2012), E1014K (Lee et al., 2015), and N617D (Dayal et al., 2017), only the voltage-sensor mutant R174W opened partially and produced tail currents under (±)Bay K 8644 administration.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The malignant hyperthermia-linked DHPR voltage-sensor mutant R174W displayed small, but clearly detectable inward Ca2+ currents together with enhanced tail currents in response to strong or prolonged depolarizations in the presence of (±)Bay K 8644.
claims.source: This malignant hyperthermia-linked DHPR voltage-sensor mutant R174W also displayed small, but clearly detectable inward Ca2+ currents together with enhanced tail currents in response to strong or prolonged depolarizations in the presence of (±)Bay K 8644 (Bannister and Beam, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: It is impossible to force either of the two DHPR pore mutants, DHPR(N617D) and DHPR(E1014K) into a Ca2+ conducting mode by executing L-type Ca2+ current amplifying conditions.
claims.source: Integrating previous and present results (Bannister and Beam, 2011), we can conclude that it is impossible to force either of the two DHPR pore mutants, DHPR(N617D) and DHPR(E1014K) into a Ca2+ conducting mode by executing the above-described L-type Ca2+ current amplifying conditions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the current study and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Under standard Ca2+ current recording conditions with 145 mM Cs+ present in the patch pipette, massive outward Cs+ currents through DHPR(E1014K) but not through DHPR(N617D) were observed.
claims.source: Specifically, under standard Ca2+ current recording conditions with 145 mM Cs+ present in the patch pipette to block K+ channels (Clay and Shlesinger, 1984), massive outward Cs+ currents through DHPR(E1014K) (Bannister and Beam, 2011; Lee et al., 2015; Beqollari et al., 2018) but not through DHPR(N617D) (Schredelseker et al., 2010; Dayal et al., 2017; Beqollari et al., 2018) were observed (see also Figure 1a, top and bottom and Figure 2b, bottom).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: At near physiological (150 mM) external Na+ as the sole monovalent cation and 10 mM external Ca2+, no slow inward Na+ currents resembling the L-type Ca2+ currents were observed in ncDHPR myotubes (n = 8).
claims.source: As demonstrated in Figure 2a and b (top), at near physiological (150 mM) external Na+ as the sole monovalent cation and 10 mM external Ca2+, no slow inward Na+ currents resembling the L-type Ca2+ currents were observed in ncDHPR myotubes (n = 8).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Upon reducing external Ca2+ from 10 to 1 mM, DHPR(N617D) remained fully impermeant to Na+ ions (n = 9).
claims.source: Even upon reducing external Ca2+ from 10 to 1 mM to lower the blocking effect by Ca2+, DHPR(N617D) remained fully impermeant to Na+ ions (Figure 2a and b, center; n = 9).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Robust slow-activating, non-inactivating inward Na+ currents were recorded from DHPR(E1014K) under comparable conditions.
claims.source: Both these observations were in stark contrast to the robust slow-activating, non-inactivating inward Na+ currents recorded from DHPR(E1014K) under comparable conditions (Bannister and Beam, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The large, rapidly activating and inactivating inward currents observed within the first ~20 ms after the onset of test potentials can be ascribed to endogenous skeletal muscle Na+ channel (NaV) isoforms.
claims.source: The large, rapidly activating and inactivating inward currents observed within the first ~20 ms after the onset of test potentials can be ascribed to endogenous skeletal muscle Na+ channel (NaV) isoforms (Numann et al., 1994) and were to a big extent, present even after administration of 2 µM Na+ channel blocker tetrodotoxin (Bannister and Beam, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and inference from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: The outward currents observed in the presence of 150 mM external Na+ can be ruled out to be Cs+ currents through DHPR(N617D) since they are blocked by the K+ channel blocker TEA+ and show kinetics very different from Cs+ currents recorded from DHPR(E1014K).
claims.source: The outward currents observed in the presence of 150 mM external Na+ (Figure 2a and b, top and center) can certainly be ruled out to be Cs+ currents through DHPR(N617D) since they are blocked by the K+ channel blocker TEA+ (Figure 2b, bottom; n = 8) and show kinetics very different from Cs+ currents recorded from DHPR(E1014K) (Lee et al., 2015; Bannister and Beam, 2011; Beqollari et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The current-voltage relationship of the outward currents which start from approximately −30 mV is linear (10 mM Ca2+: R2 = 0.99; 1 mM Ca2+: R2 = 0.97) and this together with TEA+ sensitivity strongly points to residual K+ currents through the endogenous delayed rectifier K+ channel (KV).
claims.source: Moreover, the current-voltage relationship of these currents which start from approximately −30 mV is linear (10 mM Ca2+: R2 = 0.99; 1 mM Ca2+: R2 = 0.97) and this together with TEA+ sensitivity strongly points to residual K+ currents through the endogenous delayed rectifier K+ channel (KV) (DiFranco and Vergara, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Patch-clamp recordings performed upon addition of 10 µM nifedipine to the bath solution containing 1 mM Ca2+ and 150 mM Na+ exhibited nifedipine-insensitive slow outward currents and rapidly activating and inactivating inward currents.
claims.source: As depicted in Figure 2c, patch-clamp recordings performed upon addition of 10 µM nifedipine to the bath solution containing 1 mM Ca2+ and 150 mM Na+, exhibited nifedipine-insensitive slow outward currents (Figure 2c, left) and rapidly activating and inactivating inward currents (Figure 2c, right).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: Current-voltage relationship of outward currents (no nifedipine: R2 = 0.98; with nifedipine: R2 = 0.98) as well as of inward currents (no nifedipine: Imax = −13.22 ± 1.41 pA/pF; n = 6; with nifedipine: Imax = −14.96 ± 1.40 pA/pF; n = 10) were unaffected (p>0.05) by the presence of nifedipine.
claims.source: Current-voltage relationship of outward currents (no nifedipine: R2 = 0.98; with nifedipine: R2 = 0.98) as well as of inward currents (no nifedipine: Imax = −13.22 ± 1.41 pA/pF; n = 6; with nifedipine: Imax = −14.96 ± 1.40 pA/pF; n = 10) were unaffected (p>0.05) by the presence of nifedipine.
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: DHPR(N617D) is not accountable for the outward and inward currents observed in the presence of near physiological external Na+.
claims.source: These results unambiguously confirm that DHPR(N617D) is not accountable for the outward and inward currents observed in the presence of near physiological external Na+.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the nifedipine insensitivity data presented in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: DHPR(E1014K) lost its ion-selectivity and robustly conducts monovalent anions like Cs+ as well as physiologically relevant Na+ and K+ even in the presence of physiological concentrations of external Ca2+.
claims.source: Although both DHPR pore mutants do not conduct Ca2+, DHPR(E1014K) additionally lost its ion-selectivity and robustly conducts monovalent anions like Cs+ as well as physiologically relevant Na+ and K+ even in the presence of physiological concentrations of external Ca2+.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Dirksen and Beam, 1999; Schredelseker et al., 2010; Bannister and Beam, 2011; Lee et al., 2015; Dayal et al., 2017; Beqollari et al., 2018).

claims.claim: In the presence of 100 mM extracellular Li+ and without extracellular Ca2+ block (free [Ca2+]=0), inward Li+ currents were indistinguishable (p>0.05) between ncDHPR (Imax = −2.32 ± 0.35 pA/pF; n = 16) and wt (Imax = −2.07 ± 0.47 pA/pF; n = 9) myotubes.
claims.source: In the presence of 100 mM extracellular Li+ and without extracellular Ca2+ block (free [Ca2+]=0), inward Li+ currents were indistinguishable (p>0.05) between ncDHPR (Imax = −2.32 ± 0.35 pA/pF; n = 16) and wt (Imax = −2.07 ± 0.47 pA/pF; n = 9) myotubes (Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3a.

claims.claim: Increase in extracellular Ca2+ concentration to 1 µM showed a highly significant (p<0.001) reduction of Li+ currents through ncDHPR (Imax = −0.47 ± 0.10 pA/pF; n = 8) compared to wt (Imax = −1.68 ± 0.25 pA/pF; n = 6) myotubes.
claims.source: However, increase in extracellular Ca2+ concentration to 1 µM showed a highly significant (p<0.001) reduction of Li+ currents through ncDHPR (Imax = −0.47 ± 0.10 pA/pF; n = 8) compared to wt (Imax = −1.68 ± 0.25 pA/pF; n = 6) myotubes (Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: At 3 µM external Ca2+, no Li+ currents could be evoked from ncDHPR myotubes (Imax = −0.06 ± 0.02 pA/pF; n = 7) but small, significant (p<0.001) currents through the wt DHPR (Imax = −0.24 ± 0.04 pA/pF; n = 6) were still existent.
claims.source: In particular, at 3 µM external Ca2+, no Li+ currents could be evoked from ncDHPR myotubes (Imax = −0.06 ± 0.02 pA/pF; n = 7) but small, significant (p<0.001) currents through the wt DHPR (Imax = −0.24 ± 0.04 pA/pF; n = 6) were still existent (Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: Recordings performed upon addition of 10 µM nifedipine to the bath solution containing 0 Ca2+ exhibited a drastic reduction (p<0.001) of slow inward Li+ currents (no nifedipine: Imax = −2.41 ± 0.27 pA/pF; n = 11; with nifedipine: Imax = −0.35 ± 0.13 pA/pF; n = 16).
claims.source: As depicted in Figure 4, recordings performed upon addition of 10 µM nifedipine to the bath solution containing 0 Ca2+ exhibited a drastic reduction (p<0.001) of slow inward Li+ currents (no nifedipine: Imax = −2.41 ± 0.27 pA/pF; n = 11; with nifedipine: Imax = −0.35 ± 0.13 pA/pF; n = 16).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The slow inward Li+ currents observed in the absence of external Ca2+ are mediated by DHPR(N617D).
claims.source: These results confirm that the slow inward Li+ currents observed in the absence of external Ca2+ are mediated by DHPR(N617D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the nifedipine sensitivity data presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Ca2+ block of inward Li+ currents through the skeletal muscle wt DHPR displays an IC50 of 1.57 µM (95% CI: 1.36–1.80 µM).
claims.source: As demonstrated in Figure 3d, Ca2+ block of inward Li+ currents through the skeletal muscle wt DHPR displays an IC50 of 1.57 µM (95% CI: 1.36–1.80 µM), which is highly comparable to published values of cardiac DHPR Ca2+ pore binding affinity (Yang et al., 1993; Ellinor et al., 1995; Cibulsky and Sather, 2000; Sather and McCleskey, 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3d and comparison with published values.

claims.claim: Pore mutant DHPR(N617D) exhibited an IC50 of 372.8 nM (95% CI: 334.4–415.8 nM) which is 4.2-fold shifted to lower Ca2+ concentrations.
claims.source: Interestingly, pore mutant DHPR(N617D) exhibited an IC50 of 372.8 nM (95% CI: 334.4–415.8 nM) which is indeed 4.2-fold shifted to lower Ca2+ concentrations.
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: In the mutant DHPR(N617D), introduction of the negatively charged residue D617 into the DHPR pore in close vicinity of the selectivity filter EEEE results in a significant (p<0.01) decrease in IC50 from µM to nM concentrations.
claims.source: Thus, in the mutant DHPR(N617D), introduction of the negatively charged residue D617 into the DHPR pore in close vicinity of the selectivity filter EEEE results in a significant (p<0.01) decrease in IC50 from µM to nM concentrations.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: The Hill coefficient (nH) was significantly (p<0.01) different between wt DHPR (−3.32; 95% CI: −4.68 – −2.61) and DHPR(N617D) (−1.39; 95% CI: −1.59 – −1.23).
claims.source: Notably, also the Hill coefficient (nH) was significantly (p<0.01) different between wt DHPR (−3.32; 95% CI: −4.68 – −2.61) and DHPR(N617D) (−1.39; 95% CI: −1.59 – −1.23) (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: Atypical high-affinity binding of Ca2+ to the mutant pore is incompatible with Ca2+ conductance.
claims.source: Since atypical high-affinity binding of Ca2+ to the mutant pore is apparently incompatible with Ca2+ conductance, this supports the idea of a mechanism by which the mutant DHPR(N617D) pore is occluded.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing high-affinity Ca2+ binding and lack of Ca2+ conductance.

claims.claim: In contrast to DHPR(N617D), DHPR(E1014K) functions as a slow-activating, non-inactivating, junctionally-targeted inward Na+ channel.
claims.source: Our results and earlier findings of Bannister and Beam, 2011 show that in contrast to DHPR(N617D), DHPR(E1014K) functions as a slow-activating, non-inactivating, junctionally-targeted inward Na+ channel.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the current study and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: DHPR(E1014K) has massive 1,4-DHP-sensitive, non-inactivating outward K+ conductance, which is completely absent in the DHPR(N617D) counterpart.
claims.source: However, of higher physiological relevance than this Na+ conductance of DHPR(E1014K), is probably its additional massive 1,4-DHP-sensitive, non-inactivating outward K+ conductance, which again is completely absent in the DHPR(N617D) counterpart (Beqollari et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: K+ accumulation plays a crucial role in muscle fatigue.
claims.source: K+ accumulation is known to play a crucial role in muscle fatigue (Allen et al., 2008)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In the EK mouse strain, the mutationally introduced K+ efflux from cytoplasm into the transvers (t)-tubular lumen may exacerbate muscle fatigability during periods of enhanced, repetitive activity.
claims.source: and hence, in the EK mouse strain this mutationally introduced K+ efflux from cytoplasm into the transvers (t)-tubular lumen may exacerbate muscle fatigability during periods of enhanced, repetitive activity (Beqollari et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the K+ conductance properties of DHPR(E1014K) and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: K+ overload in the t-tubule is expected to induce aberrant muscle membrane excitability, which might be the root cause for the muscle histological and metabolic aberrations observed in EK but not in ncDHPR mice.
claims.source: Additionally, K+ overload in the t-tubule is expected to induce aberrant muscle membrane excitability, which might be the root cause for the muscle histological and metabolic aberrations observed in EK (Georgiou et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2015) but not in ncDHPR mice (Dayal et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on speculation and inference from the observed phenotypic differences between the two mouse models.

claims.claim: One Ca2+ ion binds to a single high-affinity site formed by all four glutamates (EEEE locus) of the DHPR selectivity filter.
claims.source: According to this model, one Ca2+ ion binds to a single high-affinity site formed by all four glutamates (EEEE locus) of the DHPR selectivity filter.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on a widely accepted model from the literature (Yang et al., 1993; Ellinor et al., 1995; Sather and McCleskey, 2003).

claims.claim: Tight embracement of Ca2+ in the DHPR pore is a prerequisite for the high selectivity for Ca2+ over Na+, K+, or other monovalent cations.
claims.source: This tight embracement of Ca2+ in the DHPR pore is a prerequisite for the high selectivity for Ca2+ over Na+, K+, or other monovalent cations.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claims.claim: To enable rapid passage of Ca2+ through the pore, a two-site mechanism that overcomes tight Ca2+ binding is essential.
claims.source: However, to enable rapid passage of Ca2+ through the pore, a two-site mechanism that overcomes this tight Ca2+ binding is essential.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from the literature (Sather and McCleskey, 2003).

claims.claim: The EEEE locus is physically flexible and can rapidly rearrange to accommodate a pair of Ca2+ ions within the pore, but then both bound with much lower affinity (apparent KD ~14 mM).
claims.source: Accordingly, the EEEE locus has been suggested to be physically flexible. Hence, irrespective that all four selectivity filter glutamates are needed to hold a single Ca2+ ion with high affinity (KD ~1 µM), their conformation can rapidly rearrange to accommodate a pair of Ca2+ ions within the pore, but then both bound with much lower affinity (apparent KD ~14 mM).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from the literature (Sather and McCleskey, 2003).

claims.claim: The intermediate short-lived low-affinity state, together with a Ca2+- Ca2+ repulsion mechanism occurring in the doubly occupied pore, whereby one of the occupying Ca2+ ions is pushed out to the cytosolic side, is the basis for fast Ca2+ ion passage through the pore.
claims.source: This intermediate short-lived low-affinity state, together with a Ca2+- Ca2+ repulsion mechanism occurring in this doubly occupied pore, whereby one of the occupying Ca2+ ions is pushed out to the cytosolic side, is the basis for fast Ca2+ ion passage through the pore.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from the literature (Sather and McCleskey, 2003).

claims.claim: A ring of non-conserved negatively charged residues located at homologous positions in each of the four repeats of the DHPR pore, coined as 'divalent cation selectivity' (DCS) locus, is responsible for distinct channel profiles.
claims.source: In their interesting study, Cens et al., 2007 via point mutational analyses and molecular modeling identified a ring of non-conserved negatively charged residues located at homologous positions in each of the four repeats of the DHPR pore, which were responsible for the distinct channel profiles. This ring coined as 'divalent cation selectivity' (DCS) locus, is present in different constellations in every VGCC and is located towards the outer channel pore region in close vicinity of the selectivity filter EEEE locus.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Cens et al., 2007).

claims.claim: The DCS locus might constitute an additional, low-affinity Ca2+-binding site which plays a crucial role in defining and directly participating in the generation of different Ca2+ conductances in different HVA Ca2+ channels.
claims.source: The DCS locus might constitute an additional, low-affinity Ca2+-binding site which, together with distinct negative charges closely adjacent to the EEEE locus (Williamson and Sather, 1999), plays a crucial role in defining and directly participating in the generation of different Ca2+ conductances in different HVA Ca2+ channels (Cens et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Cens et al., 2007; Williamson and Sather, 1999).

claims.claim: Any substitution in the EEEE locus abolishes/decreases the high (µM) Ca2+ pore binding affinity as demonstrated by Ca2+ block of Li+ current experiments.
claims.source: Any substitution in the EEEE locus abolishes/decreases this high (µM) Ca2+ pore binding affinity as demonstrated by Ca2+ block of Li+ current experiments (Yang et al., 1993; Ellinor et al., 1995; Sather and McCleskey, 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The EIIIK mutation drastically reduced the pore's affinity for Ca2+ to 1000-fold, as is depicted by an increase in IC50 from ~1 µM to ~1 mM for Ca2+ block of ILi+.
claims.source: Specifically, the strongest impact on the binding affinity was produced by exchange of E in repeat III. The EIIIK mutation drastically reduced the pore's affinity for Ca2+ to 1000-fold, as is depicted by an increase in IC50 from ~1 µM to ~1 mM for Ca2+ block of ILi+ (Yang et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The large outward Cs+ current found in the skeletal muscle EIIIK mutant DHPR(E1014K), which was not blocked even in the presence of 10 mM external Ca2+, was interpreted as an indication of very little residual Ca2+ binding within the DHPR(E1014K) pore.
claims.source: Accordingly, the large outward Cs+ current found in the skeletal muscle EIIIK mutant DHPR(E1014K) (Bannister and Beam, 2011; Lee et al., 2015; Beqollari et al., 2018), which was not blocked even in the presence of 10 mM external Ca2+, was consequently interpreted as an indication of very little residual Ca2+ binding within the DHPR(E1014K) pore (Dirksen and Beam, 1999; Beqollari et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: A considerable inward Na+ current through EK myotubes despite external Ca2+ concentration as high as 10 mM indicates a very marginal, low-affinity binding of Ca2+ within the DHPR(E1014K) pore.
claims.source: Similarly, a considerable inward Na+ current through EK myotubes despite external Ca2+ concentration as high as 10 mM (Bannister and Beam, 2011) again indicates a very marginal, low-affinity binding of Ca2+ within the DHPR(E1014K) pore.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and inference.

claims.claim: Low-affinity pore-bound Ca2+ is unable to block the flux of any cation in both directions and hence Ca2+ selectivity is abolished in the mutant DHPR(E1014K).
claims.source: Consequently, low-affinity pore-bound Ca2+ is unable to block the flux of any cation in both directions and hence Ca2+ selectivity is abolished in the mutant DHPR(E1014K).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the properties of DHPR(E1014K).

claims.claim: Since the EEEE locus is mutated to EEKE in DHPR(E1014K), attraction of a second Ca2+ and subsequent competition for binding valences with the Ca2+ ion that is already bound with low affinity to this EEKE locus is impossible.
claims.source: In addition, since the EEEE locus is mutated to EEKE, attraction of a second Ca2+ and subsequent competition for binding valences with the Ca2+ ion that is already bound with low affinity to this EEKE locus is impossible.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the structural change in the selectivity filter.

claims.claim: Absence of the intermediate doubly occupied pore and thus, of the Ca2+- Ca2+ repulsion mechanism as the basis for fast, unidirectional Ca2+ ion passage through the pore is sufficient to explain the lack of Ca2+ conductance through the mutant DHPR(E1014K).
claims.source: Absence of this intermediate doubly occupied pore and thus, of the Ca2+- Ca2+ repulsion mechanism as the basis for fast, unidirectional Ca2+ ion passage through the pore is sufficient to explain the lack of Ca2+ conductance through the mutant DHPR(E1014K).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: Ca2+ ions from the t-tubular (extracellular) side are attracted to the negative charges of the DCS locus, which in mouse DHPRα1S is formed by D296 of repeat I, E1327 of repeat IV, and supported by D615 of repeat II.
claims.source: According to our postulated pore model (Figure 5a), Ca2+ ions from the t-tubular (extracellular) side are attracted to the negative charges of the DCS locus, which in mouse DHPRα1S is formed by D296 of repeat I, E1327 of repeat IV, and supported by D615 of repeat II.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the proposed model illustrated in Figure 5a.

claims.claim: The loosely bound Ca2+ ion at the DCS locus is easily mobilized (probably by charge repulsion from excess Ca2+ ions in the t-tubule) and migrates deeper into the pore to compete with the tightly bound Ca2+ ion for binding valences of the EEEE locus.
claims.source: This loosely bound Ca2+ ion is easily mobilized (probably by charge repulsion from excess Ca2+ ions in the t-tubule) and migrates deeper into the pore to compete with the tightly bound Ca2+ ion for binding valences of the EEEE locus (in mouse skeletal-muscle DHPR: E292, E614, E1014, E1323).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the proposed model and speculation about the mechanism.

claims.claim: Due to the reduced binding (µM to mM affinity), Ca2+- Ca2+ repulsion takes place, eventually pushing the loosely bound Ca2+ into the cytosol.
claims.source: Henceforth, due to the reduced binding (µM to mM affinity), Ca2+- Ca2+ repulsion (Sather and McCleskey, 2003) takes place, eventually pushing the loosely bound Ca2+ into the cytosol.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the proposed model and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Molecular dynamics simulations show that the EEEE locus attracts and stabilizes a single Ca2+ ion.
claims.source: This conceptual model is supported by simulation experiments as depicted in Figure 6. Molecular dynamics simulations show that the EEEE locus attracts and stabilizes a single Ca2+ ion (Figure 6b–c).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by molecular dynamics simulation data presented in Figure 6.

claims.claim: In the wt DHPR, conformational changes in the EEEE locus allow binding of a second Ca2+ ion, resulting in weaker binding of the glutamate residues to both Ca2+ ions and causing repulsion between the two ions.
claims.source: However, in the wt DHPR we also observe conformational changes in the EEEE locus that allow binding of a second Ca2+ ion. This additional Ca2+ ion results in a weaker binding of the glutamate residues to both Ca2+ ions, thereby causing a repulsion between the two ions, which is reflected in their decreasing distance to as low as 6 Å (Figure 6c, left).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by molecular dynamics simulation data presented in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Metadynamics simulations show that as a consequence of Ca2+ - Ca2+ repulsion occurring in the doubly occupied EEEE locus, one of the two Ca2+ ions moves toward the cytosolic side.
claims.source: Furthermore, metadynamics simulations show that as a consequence of this Ca2+ - Ca2+ repulsion occurring in the doubly occupied EEEE locus, one of the two Ca2+ ions moves toward the cytosolic side (Figure 6c, left; Figure 6—video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by metadynamics simulation data presented in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The weaker binding of the Ca2+ ions to the EEEE locus of the wt DHPR compared to the mutant DHPR(N617D) is reflected in the significantly (p<0.001) lower free energy barrier.
claims.source: The weaker binding of the Ca2+ ions to the EEEE locus of the wt DHPR compared to the mutant DHPR(N617D), is reflected in the significantly (p<0.001) lower free energy barrier (Figure 6d).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by metadynamics simulation data presented in Figure 6d.

claims.claim: The additional negative charge D617 in mutant DHPR(N617D), introduced in close vicinity to the residue D615 in repeat II, creates an additional binding valence and induces an aberrant high Ca2+ binding-affinity to the DCS locus.
claims.source: Contrary to this smooth Ca2+- conducting mechanism of wt DHPR, the additional negative charge D617 in mutant DHPR(N617D), introduced in the close vicinity to the residue D615 in repeat II (Figure 5b), creates an additional binding valence and as a result induces an aberrant high Ca2+ binding-affinity to the DCS locus.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the structural change and the proposed model illustrated in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: The tighter bound Ca2+ at the DCS locus in DHPR(N617D) is not sufficiently mobile to travel deeper into the pore to compete for the binding valences of the selectivity-filter EEEE locus with the already strongly bound Ca2+ ion.
claims.source: According to our model, this considerably tighter bound Ca2+ is consequently not sufficiently mobile anymore to travel deeper into the pore to compete for the binding valences of the selectivity-filter EEEE locus with the already strongly bound Ca2+ ion.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proposed model.

claims.claim: Lack of formation of the intermediate short-lived lower-affinity Ca2+ binding state, together with the consequential lack of Ca2+- Ca2+ repulsion at the EEEE locus explains the absence of Ca2+ influx through the DHPR(N617D) pore.
claims.source: Overall, lack of formation of the intermediate short-lived lower-affinity Ca2+ binding state, together with the consequential lack of Ca2+- Ca2+ repulsion at the EEEE locus explicitly explains the absence of Ca2+ influx through the DHPR(N617D) pore.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proposed model.

claims.claim: Molecular dynamics simulations show that immediately after the equilibration step, one Ca2+ ion is stabilized at the EEEE locus while the other Ca2+ is bound to the DCS locus in DHPR(N617D).
claims.source: Congruently, molecular dynamics simulations show that immediately after the equilibration step, one Ca2+ ion is stabilized at the EEEE locus while the other Ca2+ is bound to the DCS locus (Figure 6c, right; Figure 6—video 2).

claims.claim: The translocation of the Ca2+ ions to the DCS and EEEE locus in DHPR(N617D) occurs within 1 ns of simulation time succeeding the last step of the equilibration protocol.
claims.source: This translocation of the Ca2+ ions to the DCS and EEEE locus occurs already within 1 ns of simulation time succeeding the last step of the equilibration protocol.

claims.claim: The distance between the two Ca2+ ions in DHPR(N617D) is ~9 Å.
claims.source: Here, the distance between the two Ca2+ ions is ~9 Å.
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claims.claim: The strong binding of the two Ca2+ ions to the EEEE and DCS locus makes it impossible for any other ion, like Li+, to pass through the DHPR(N617D) pore.
claims.source: The strong binding of the two Ca2+ ions to the EEEE and DCS locus makes it impossible for any other ion, like Li+, to pass through the DHPR(N617D) pore.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the simulation data.

claims.claim: Simulations of pulling of Ca2+ ions through the selectivity filter of mutant DHPR(N617D) result in a significantly (p<0.001), ~8 times higher energy barrier compared to wt DHPR.
claims.source: Thus, simulations of pulling of Ca2+ ions through the selectivity filter of mutant DHPR(N617D) result in a significantly (p<0.001), ~8 times higher energy barrier compared to wt DHPR (Figure 6d), which is in accordance with the experimentally observed complete occlusion of the DHPR(N617D) pore in the presence of physiological concentrations of extracellular Ca2+ ions (Figure 3).

claims.source: The Hill slope/Hill coefficient (nH) derived from four parameter logistic fit of dose-response curve is best portrayed as an 'interaction' coefficient, reflecting the extent of cooperativity among multiple binding sites (Prinz, 2010).

claims.claim: The considerably more dynamic Ca2+ interactions in the wt DHPR pore with its successive short-lived intermediate high and low binding affinities and repulsion mechanisms are apparent in the higher nH compared to DHPR(N617D).
claims.source: The considerably more dynamic Ca2+ interactions in the wt DHPR pore with its successive short-lived intermediate high and low binding affinities and repulsion mechanisms are consequently apparent in the higher nH compared to DHPR(N617D).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and the proposed model.

claims.claim: Point mutation N617D was originally identified to be responsible for DHPR Ca2+ non-conductivity in zebrafish fast (glycolytic/white) skeletal muscle.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: During vertebrate evolution (from mammalian species to teleost fishes) a steady loss of DHPR Ca2+ conductance occurred.
claims.source: Additionally, with studies on the low-Ca2+ conducting DHPR of sterlet (Acipenser ruthenus), which is phylogenetically somewhere in between mouse and zebrafish, we showed (Schrötter et al., 2017) that during vertebrate evolution (i.e. from the mammalian species, e.g. mouse, to the teleost fishes, e.g. zebrafish) a steady loss of DHPR Ca2+ conductance occurred.

claims.claim: During evolution from mammals to teleost fishes an accumulation of DHPR amino acid exchanges occurred that contributed to the reduction of Ca2+ conductance.
claims.source: Subsuming results of several studies, we proposed the hypothesis that during evolution from mammals to teleost fishes an accumulation of DHPR amino acid exchanges occurred that contributed to the reduction of Ca2+ conductance (Schredelseker et al., 2010; Dayal et al., 2017; Schrötter et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Mutation N→D (N617D; mouse numbering) that finally 'turned off' the already reduced Ca2+ conductance evolved only in quite a late phylogenetic stage, following the teleost-specific third round (Ts3R) of gene duplication.
claims.source: Mutation N→D (N617D; mouse numbering) that finally 'turned off' the already reduced Ca2+ conductance evolved only in quite a late phylogenetic stage (Dayal et al., 2017; Schrötter et al., 2017), following the teleost-specific third round (Ts3R) of gene duplication (Meyer and Van de Peer, 2005; Glasauer and Neuhauss, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The evolutionary pressure that caused substantial modifications in skeletal muscle organization and physiology in teleost fishes arose from the critical demand for tighter controlled, faster and stronger muscle contractions, crucial for high-speed movements in the aquatic prey-predator environment.
claims.source: Beside DHPR non-conductivity, the evolutionary pressure that caused additional substantial modifications in skeletal muscle organization and physiology in teleost fishes (Schredelseker et al., 2010; Dayal et al., 2017; Schrötter et al., 2017) arose from the critical demand for tighter controlled, faster and stronger muscle contractions, crucial for high-speed movements in the aquatic prey-predator environment (Dayal et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Ts3R headed into the evolution of a second DHPR isoform in zebrafish slow (oxidative/red) skeletal muscle that is likewise Ca2+ non-conducting.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.source: This slow muscle DHPR is so far the only described innate DHPR with a distorted EEEE locus, where glutamate of repeat I is substituted by glutamine.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Schredelseker et al., 2010).

claims.claim: Exchange of selectivity filter E292 with Q in a GFP-tagged rabbit DHPRα1S clone yielded mutant DHPR(E292Q), which upon heterologous expression in dysgenic myotubes confirmed the abolishment of inward Ca2+ currents.
claims.source: Exchange of this selectivity filter E292 with Q in a GFP-tagged rabbit DHPRα1S clone (Grabner et al., 1998) yielded mutant DHPR(E292Q), which upon heterologous expression in dysgenic myotubes confirmed the abolishment of inward Ca2+ currents (Schredelseker et al., 2010) with a slight outward Cs+ current, typically starting at +20 to+30 mV (Bannister and Beam, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The EQ pore mutation in repeat I of the cardiac DHPR exerted a minor effect, as the increase in IC50 was only twofold compared to the wt.

claims.claim: Appropriate Ca2+ pore-affinity essential for proper Ca2+ selectivity and Ca2+ conductance must exist in a surprisingly small range, somewhere between approximately 0.37 (IC50 for N617D) and 3.2 µM (2-fold IC50 for wt).
claims.source: Incorporation of our present and previously published data (Yang et al., 1993; Schredelseker et al., 2010) indicates that this small range might be within approximately one order of magnitude, somewhere between 0.37 (IC50 for N617D) and 3.2 µM (2-fold IC50 for wt).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current experimental data and previous work.

claims.claim: The hampered Ca2+ selectivity and conductance mechanism of mutant DHPR(E292Q) is essentially the same as for DHPR(E1014K).
claims.source: The hampered Ca2+ selectivity and conductance mechanism of mutant DHPR(E292Q) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a) is expected to be essentially the same as discussed above for DHPR(E1014K).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proposed model.

claims.claim: Low-affinity Ca2+ binding to the QEEE locus cannot support the crucial Ca2+ - Ca2+ repulsion mechanism and thus, Ca2+ conductance through mutant DHPR(E292Q) is blocked.
claims.source: In brief, low-affinity Ca2+ binding to the QEEE locus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a) cannot support the crucial Ca2+ - Ca2+ repulsion mechanism and thus, Ca2+ conductance through mutant DHPR(E292Q) is blocked.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proposed model.

claims.claim: Ca2+ block of the bidirectional flux of monovalent cations, and hence Ca2+ selectivity is abolished in DHPR(E292Q).
claims.source: Likewise, Ca2+ block of the bidirectional flux of monovalent cations, and hence Ca2+ selectivity is abolished.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proposed model.

claims.claim: In early phylogenetic teleost species (including zebrafish from the order cypriniformes) mutation N→D (N617D, mouse numbering) is the archetypical mutation to block DHPR Ca2+ influx.
claims.source: Although in the early phylogenetic teleost species (including zebrafish from the order cypriniformes) mutation N→D (N617D, mouse numbering) is the archetypical mutation to block DHPR Ca2+ influx, in phylogenetically higher developed teleost species starting with the order lophiiformes (anglerfishes), this negatively charged D was lost by mutating to a neutral T (Schredelseker et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In phylogenetically higher developed teleost species starting with the order lophiiformes (anglerfishes), the negatively charged D was lost by mutating to a neutral T.
claims.source: Although in the early phylogenetic teleost species (including zebrafish from the order cypriniformes) mutation N→D (N617D, mouse numbering) is the archetypical mutation to block DHPR Ca2+ influx, in phylogenetically higher developed teleost species starting with the order lophiiformes (anglerfishes), this negatively charged D was lost by mutating to a neutral T (Schredelseker et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.source: Concurrent to this D→T mutation, DHPR Ca2+ non-conductivity was re-installed by mutation of another D, which is one of the negative charges in the DCS locus (located in pore repeat I) and highly homologous in all mammalian L-type Ca2+ channels, to positively charged K (D→K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Schredelseker et al., 2010).

claims.claim: Exchange of DCS locus D296 with K in a GFP-tagged rabbit DHPRα1S clone yielded mutant DHPR(D296K), which upon heterologous expression in dysgenic myotubes was sufficient to abolish inward Ca2+ currents.
claims.source: As demonstrated previously (Schredelseker et al., 2010), exchange of this DCS locus D296 with K in a GFP-tagged rabbit DHPRα1S clone yielded mutant DHPR(D296K). Upon heterologous expression in dysgenic myotubes, this single charge conversion was sufficient to abolish inward Ca2+ currents.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: K296 does not permit formation of an active DCS locus, and thus Ca2+ from the t-tubular (extracellular) space is no more attracted to the DCS locus.
claims.source: According to our combined model of Ca2+ selectivity and conductance and illustrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b, K296 does not permit formation of an active DCS locus, and thus Ca2+ from the t-tubular (extracellular) space is no more attracted to the DCS locus.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proposed model illustrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claims.claim: There is lack of easy to mobilize low-affine DCS-bound Ca2+ that would compete with the tightly EEEE-bound Ca2+ for the binding valences of the EEEE locus in DHPR(D296K).
claims.source: Resultantly, there is lack of easy to mobilize low-affine DCS-bound Ca2+ that would compete with the tightly EEEE-bound Ca2+ for the binding valences of the EEEE locus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proposed model.

claims.claim: The Ca2+- Ca2+ repulsion mechanism and pushing out of the Ca2+ bound to the selectivity filter into the cytosol cannot take place in DHPR(D296K).
claims.source: Thus, the Ca2+- Ca2+ repulsion mechanism (Sather and McCleskey, 2003) and pushing out of the Ca2+ bound to the selectivity filter into the cytosol cannot take place.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proposed model and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The charge conversion D296K in blocking of inward DHPR Ca2+ flux proves the importance of the DCS locus for proper inward DHPR Ca2+ currents in skeletal muscle.
claims.source: The surprising implication of charge conversion D296K in blocking of inward DHPR Ca2+ flux proves the importance of the DCS locus for proper inward DHPR Ca2+ currents in skeletal muscle and consequently, fundamentally supports our model of DHPR Ca2+ selectivity and Ca2+ conductivity.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on DHPR(D296K) and the proposed model.

results.result: DHPR(N617D) remains Ca2+ impermeant even under conditions known to augment L-type Ca2+ currents, including Bay K 8644 administration, strong depolarizations, and prolonged depolarizations.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C20-C26, and C32 collectively demonstrate through multiple experimental protocols (Bay K 8644, strong depolarizations to +90 mV, and 2 s depolarizations) that DHPR(N617D) does not conduct Ca2+ under any current-enhancing conditions tested, while wt DHPR shows robust Ca2+ currents. The data are internally consistent with appropriate controls and statistical significance (p<0.001 to p<0.01).

results.result: DHPR(N617D) does not conduct Na+ currents under near-physiological conditions (150 mM external Na+, 1-10 mM Ca2+), as confirmed by nifedipine insensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 and C43-C45 demonstrate through patch-clamp recordings and pharmacological blockade with nifedipine that DHPR(N617D) does not mediate Na+ currents. The nifedipine insensitivity (C44, p>0.05) provides strong evidence that observed currents are not through DHPR(N617D), supporting the conclusion in C45.

results.result: DHPR(N617D) exhibits 4.2-fold higher Ca2+ pore-binding affinity (IC50 = 372.8 nM) compared to wt DHPR (IC50 = 1.57 µM), as demonstrated by Ca2+ block of Li+ current experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C55 present a comprehensive dose-response analysis with appropriate statistical testing (p<0.001 to p<0.01) and confidence intervals. The Li+ current experiments (C47-C49) show progressive Ca2+-dependent block, nifedipine sensitivity confirms DHPR mediation (C50-C51), and the IC50 determination (C52-C53) is well-supported by the data in Table 1 and Figure 3d. The Hill coefficient difference (C55) adds mechanistic insight.

results.result: Molecular dynamics and metadynamics simulations demonstrate that wt DHPR allows Ca2+-Ca2+ repulsion and ion passage through the EEEE locus, while DHPR(N617D) exhibits ~8-fold higher energy barrier (122 ± 20 vs 15 ± 4 kcal/mol) with Ca2+ ions stabilized at both DCS and EEEE loci.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 and C86-C91 present computational evidence that complements the experimental findings. The simulations show mechanistic differences between wt and mutant channels with statistically significant energy barriers (p<0.001, C90-C91). The simulations are appropriately described with methods (equilibration, metadynamics parameters) and replicate numbers (n=5), though validation against experimental structures or independent computational methods would strengthen confidence.

results.result: A molecular model proposes cooperativity between the DCS locus (outer pore) and EEEE locus (central pore), where the N617D mutation increases Ca2+ binding affinity at the DCS locus, preventing Ca2+ mobilization and the Ca2+-Ca2+ repulsion mechanism required for conductance.
results.evaluation: Claims C18 and C76-C85 present a mechanistic model integrating experimental and computational data. The model is supported by the IC50 shift (C14, C53-C54), simulation data (C79-C91), and prior literature on Ca2+ channel selectivity. While the model involves inference and speculation (C77, C84), it is well-grounded in the experimental observations and provides a coherent explanation for the phenotypic differences between DHPR(N617D) and DHPR(E1014K).

results.result: DHPR(E1014K) conducts Cs+, Na+, and K+ currents and has lost ion selectivity, contrasting with DHPR(N617D) which maintains selectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C36, C46, C57-C58 are supported by citations to multiple previous studies (Bannister and Beam, 2011; Lee et al., 2015; Beqollari et al., 2018; Dirksen and Beam, 1999; Schredelseker et al., 2010; Dayal et al., 2017) and data presented in Figures 1-2. This establishes the key functional difference between the two mutants that explains their divergent phenotypes.

results.result: K+ efflux through DHPR(E1014K) may exacerbate muscle fatigability and induce aberrant membrane excitability, potentially explaining the muscle aberrations in EK but not ncDHPR mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 are speculative (evidence_type includes SPECULATION and INFERENCE) and rely on inference from K+ conductance properties and phenotypic differences. While the hypothesis is plausible and grounded in established muscle physiology (C59), direct experimental evidence linking K+ efflux to the observed phenotypes is lacking. The authors appropriately use cautious language ('may', 'might', 'expected').

results.result: The manuscript describes established models of Ca2+ channel selectivity and permeation, including the EEEE locus high-affinity binding, two-site mechanism, and the DCS locus role in defining Ca2+ conductance.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C68 accurately summarize well-established knowledge from the literature (Yang et al., 1993; Ellinor et al., 1995; Sather and McCleskey, 2003; Cens et al., 2007; Williamson and Sather, 1999). These are appropriately cited background claims that provide the foundation for the authors' model.

results.result: The EIIIK mutation (E1014K) drastically reduces Ca2+ pore binding affinity to mM range, abolishing Ca2+ selectivity and conductance through loss of the Ca2+-Ca2+ repulsion mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C75 integrate prior literature (Yang et al., 1993; Bannister and Beam, 2011; Lee et al., 2015; Beqollari et al., 2018; Dirksen and Beam, 1999) with inference to explain the DHPR(E1014K) phenotype. The mechanism is well-supported by the cited studies showing low-affinity Ca2+ binding and loss of selectivity.

results.result: The lower Hill coefficient in DHPR(N617D) compared to wt DHPR reflects less dynamic Ca2+ interactions in the mutant pore.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 provide mechanistic interpretation of the Hill coefficient difference (C55). The interpretation is grounded in established understanding of Hill coefficients as interaction/cooperativity measures (C93, Prinz, 2010) and is consistent with the proposed model of static vs. dynamic Ca2+ binding.

results.result: The N617D mutation evolved in teleost fishes following the teleost-specific third round of gene duplication, as part of evolutionary modifications for faster muscle contractions in the aquatic environment.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C100 are supported by citations to previous work (Schredelseker et al., 2010; Dayal et al., 2017; Schrötter et al., 2017; Meyer and Van de Peer, 2005; Glasauer and Neuhauss, 2014; Dayal et al., 2019). These claims provide evolutionary context for the N617D mutation and are appropriately cited.

results.result: The zebrafish slow muscle DHPR(E292Q) mutation in the EEEE locus abolishes Ca2+ conductance through a mechanism similar to DHPR(E1014K), with appropriate Ca2+ pore-affinity existing in a narrow range (0.37-3.2 µM).
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C107 integrate prior work (Schredelseker et al., 2010; Yang et al., 1993; Bannister and Beam, 2011; Grabner et al., 1998) with current data to define the permissive range for Ca2+ conductance. The inference about the E292Q mechanism (C105-C107) is reasonable based on the established model, though it is not directly tested in this study.

results.result: In phylogenetically advanced teleost species, the D296K mutation in the DCS locus blocks Ca2+ conductance by preventing Ca2+ attraction to the DCS locus, supporting the importance of the DCS locus for Ca2+ currents.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C115 are supported by citations to previous work (Schredelseker et al., 2010) showing that the D296K mutation abolishes Ca2+ currents. The mechanistic interpretation (C112-C114) is based on inference from the proposed model but is consistent with the experimental observation. This provides additional support for the DCS-EEEE cooperativity model.

results.result: Skeletal muscle EC coupling is Ca2+-influx-independent and operates through DICR, contrasting with cardiac CICR.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C6-C8 accurately describe well-established concepts in muscle physiology, supported by foundational citations (Armstrong et al., 1972; Schneider and Chandler, 1973; Rios and Brum, 1987; Lamb, 2000; Endo, 1977; Palade and Györke, 1993; Bers, 2002). These provide essential background for the study.

results.result: Two mouse models with Ca2+ non-conducting DHPRs, DHPR(N617D) and DHPR(E1014K), show contradictory phenotypes despite both blocking Ca2+ influx.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 and C9-C12 accurately describe the motivation for the study, citing the relevant prior work (Lee et al., 2015; Dayal et al., 2017; Georgiou et al., 2015; Schredelseker et al., 2010; Bannister and Beam, 2011; Beqollari et al., 2018). This establishes the scientific problem addressed by the manuscript.

results.result: L-type Ca2+ channels undergo mode 2 gating in response to DHP agonists or strong/prolonged depolarizations, but neither DHPR pore mutant (N617D or E1014K) can be forced into Ca2+ conducting mode by these conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C31 and C33-C35 describe established L-type Ca2+ channel behavior (Hess et al., 1984; Wilkens et al., 2001; Pietrobon and Hess, 1990; Bannister and Beam, 2013) and integrate this with current and prior data (Eltit et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2015; Dayal et al., 2017; Bannister and Beam, 2011) to conclude that the pore mutants cannot be forced into conducting mode.

results.result: Rapidly activating/inactivating inward currents in ncDHPR myotubes are attributable to endogenous NaV channels, while slow outward currents are residual K+ currents through KV channels, not DHPR(N617D).
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 provide appropriate interpretation of contaminating currents based on kinetics, TEA+ sensitivity, and linear I-V relationship (R²=0.97-0.99), with citations to relevant literature (Numann et al., 1994; Bannister and Beam, 2011; Lee et al., 2015; Beqollari et al., 2018; DiFranco and Vergara, 2011). This is important for ruling out alternative explanations.

results.result: Atypical high-affinity Ca2+ binding to the mutant DHPR(N617D) pore is incompatible with Ca2+ conductance, supporting a pore occlusion mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 is a reasonable inference from the experimental data showing high-affinity Ca2+ binding (C14, C53-C54) and lack of Ca2+ conductance (C13, C32). This conclusion integrates the experimental observations into a coherent mechanistic explanation.
